description:
The DataVault benchmark's hash key columns are defined as VARCHAR(32), sized for
MD5's 32-char hex output. MD5 has known collision vulnerabilities that make it
unsuitable for Data Vault 2.0 in any production-representative benchmark - the
whole point of DV2.0 hash keys is collision-free surrogate identity.

A root-cause analysis revealed a five-layer inconsistency across the codebase:

  1. BenchmarkOptionSpec (benchmark.py:485) declares choices=("md5", "sha256") -
     the CLI accepts sha256 and the docs advertise it.
  2. SUPPORTED_HASH_ALGORITHMS = ("md5",) (benchmark.py:56) immediately rejects
     sha256 at construction time with ValueError.
  3. HashAlgorithm = Literal["md5"] (hash_functions.py:16) narrows the type to
     match the runtime - the unreachable sha1/sha256 branches were cleaned up in
     fc6509c35 along with the [:32] truncation; sha256 must now be added back cleanly.
  4. (Resolved by fc6509c35) The sha256 branch truncated to [:32], destroying
     half the entropy. That branch is gone; the function now raises ValueError for
     non-md5 inputs. Remaining work is to add sha256 properly post-schema migration.
  5. DataVaultETLTransformer hard-codes `if hash_algorithm != "md5"` (transformer.py:136)
     independently of SUPPORTED_HASH_ALGORITHMS.

The fix has two sequential phases: (a) immediately stop the CLI from advertising
sha256 while the schema cannot support it, and (b) migrate the schema to VARCHAR(64)
and wire sha256 through all remaining layers cleanly.

After this work, `benchbox run --platform duckdb --benchmark datavault
--benchmark-option hash_algorithm=sha256` must execute successfully end-to-end.

anti_patterns.why: 40-char output doesn't map to either VARCHAR(32) or VARCHAR(64) cleanly, and SHA-1 offers no security advantage over SHA-256

anti_patterns.dont: add a second HASHKEY_WIDE column type alongside HASHKEY
anti_patterns.instead: change HASHKEY in place since VARCHAR(64) is backward-compatible
anti_patterns.why: that creates two parallel schema paths that diverge

anti_patterns.dont: keep the [:32] truncation as a compatibility shim
anti_patterns.instead: remove it entirely once VARCHAR(64) lands
anti_patterns.why: it destroys entropy and makes SHA-256 no better than MD5

anti_patterns.dont: replicate the algorithm check in each layer independently
anti_patterns.why: that is the root cause of this entire bug

preserves.behavior: Existing VARCHAR(32) test fixtures remain valid - stored MD5 hashes are still 32 chars and fit in VARCHAR(64) without truncation
MD5 remains the default - hash_algorithm defaults to 'md5' in all constructors and CLI options
SHA-1 stays unsupported - 40-char output doesn't align with either VARCHAR(32) or VARCHAR(64), and SHA-1 is cryptographically weaker than SHA-256
generate_hash_key_sql() remains MD5-only - DuckDB's md5() SQL function is the only hash SQL available without custom extensions; that restriction stands

Exact changes in order:

1. hash_functions.py:16 - widen type:
     HashAlgorithm = Literal["md5", "sha256"]
   SHA-1 stays excluded: it's neither collision-safe nor schema-compatible (40 chars).

2. hash_functions.py:43-45 - add sha256 branch before the raise:
     (The old truncated [:32] sha256 branch was removed in fc6509c35;
      the function body is now just md5 + raise ValueError.)
     Add:
       elif algorithm == "sha256":
           return hashlib.sha256(key_string.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()
     The 64-char output fits VARCHAR(64).

3. benchmark.py:56 - widen the allowlist:
     SUPPORTED_HASH_ALGORITHMS = ("md5", "sha256")

4. benchmark.py:485 - restore sha256 in CLI choices:
     choices=("md5", "sha256")

5. transformer.py:136-137 - replace the hard-coded check with a reference:
     from benchbox.core.datavault.benchmark import DataVaultBenchmark
     if hash_algorithm not in DataVaultBenchmark.SUPPORTED_HASH_ALGORITHMS:
         raise ValueError(...)
   Or import SUPPORTED_HASH_ALGORITHMS directly to avoid circular import.

SHA-1 is deliberately not added: 40-char output doesn't map cleanly to
either VARCHAR(32) or VARCHAR(64), and SHA-1 is cryptographically weaker
than SHA-256.
